query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, adherent anti‐oxidation coating (for example, an aluminide or silicide layer) to the surface of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will significantly improve its resistance to oxygen uptake (thereby mitigating pesting) during high‐temperature exposure without compromising its room‐temperature tensile ductility and high‐temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C (strain rates between 10−4 and 10−2 s−1), but with inadequate oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: A single surface treatment: the application of a thin, high‐purity anti‐oxidation coating (e.g., via electrospark deposition or pack cementation to form an aluminide/silicide layer).
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours; mechanical testing at room temperature and at high temperature (e.g., 1000 °C) under the specified strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dense, slow-growing oxide scale (such as Al2O3 or a comparable protective silicide/aluminide layer) at the coated surface that retards oxygen diffusion into the alloy substrate.
generation.mechanism: The protective coating acts as a barrier that prevents or greatly slows the ingress of oxygen at high temperatures, thereby inhibiting the formation of deleterious oxides (pesting) while not altering the bulk microstructure that underpins the alloy’s desirable mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated samples will exhibit a markedly reduced oxygen uptake during 5-hour exposure at 800 °C and retain comparable (or minimally affected) room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength relative to the uncoated material.
generation.baseline: Uncoated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr, which shows insufficient oxygen resistance (pesting) at high temperatures despite good mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable for high-temperature (near 800 °C) oxidizing environments over exposure times of around 5 hours, and under tensile loading conditions representative of the alloy’s current performance envelope.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the long-term adhesion and thermal cycling durability of the coating and its potential to affect stress distributions at the surface. Also uncertain is whether the coating process might inadvertently alter the near-surface microstructure in a way that could affect mechanical performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples: one set with the applied thin anti‐oxidation coating (using a chosen method that forms an aluminide/silicide barrier) and one uncoated control set. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, perform microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM/EDS) to quantify oxide layer thickness and oxygen penetration, and conduct mechanical tests at room temperature and at elevated temperature (near 1000 °C) at defined strain rates.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and composition (via SEM/EDS, XRD)
High-temperature yield strength under specified strain rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples show oxygen penetration, pesting, or oxide scale development at levels similar to or worse than the uncoated samples—and/or if the coating adversely affects the alloy’s tensile ductility or yield strength (i.e., changes exceed acceptable variances)—then the hypothesis that the coating improves oxygen resistance without degrading mechanical performance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.

HfNbTaTiZr is a high-entropy alloy, and according to a calculated VEC value of 4.4, it has a body-centered cubic (BCC) structure. The alloy was developed by mechanical alloying from high-purity metallic powders in a Pulverisette 6 classic line planetary ball mill (Fritsch®, Idar-Oberstein, Germany) with a stainless steel vial and grinding media. Due to the powder reactivity, handling and alloying were performed under an argon atmosphere. To avoid the welding of the alloy to the vial and balls and to reduce the oxidation and contamination of powders, n-heptane was used as a control process agent (PCA). Milling parameters were selected after multiple trials to ensure that the powders were not overheating. A mixture of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr high-purity powders was milled for 60 h, and samples were taken at different time intervals to evaluate the alloying degree. After the alloying process, the particle size was reduced, and a good homogeneity was obtained. With further processing represented by sintering and deposition, the alloying degree was increased.
